chunks.heading: What is demand?
chunks.body: Demand is the amount of something people are willing and able to buy, at a certain price, at a certain time.

chunks.heading: Goods that replace each other
chunks.body: Substitutes are goods people swap for one another, like butter and margarine. If the price of one substitute rises, demand for the other tends to rise too.

chunks.body: If people expect a good's price to rise soon, they often buy more of it now. This pushes current demand up, even before the price actually changes.

chunks.body: As people's tastes and preferences change over time, so does their demand. A new trend or new technology can make a product suddenly more or less wanted.

chunks.body: Economists study demand by changing one factor, like price, while assuming every other factor stays the same. This assumption is called ceteris paribus.

chunks.body: Demand is elastic when quantity demanded changes a lot for a small price change. It's inelastic when quantity demanded barely changes at all.

chunks.heading: Necessities vs luxuries
chunks.body: Necessities, like bread, have inelastic demand because people keep buying them even if the price rises. Luxuries have more elastic demand, since people can easily go without them.
